cards.title: Losing a Shark Tank Deal to a Higher Valuation
cards.summary: A strong Shark Tank pitch can attract outside capital at a higher valuation than the on-show offer, so investors may be outbid.
cards.use_when: Preparing for a pitch or evaluating whether a TV pitch is your best fundraising route.

cards.title: Why a Founder Should Not Judge Pitches Too Harshly
cards.summary: Most early-stage pitches are rough, and the founder's job is to identify potential rather than dismiss founders for lack of polish.
cards.use_when: Evaluating early-stage businesses or preparing for your own first pitch.

cards.title: Agency exit multiples: what drives valuation
cards.summary: An agency owner breaks down the factors behind exit multiples, from client quality to retention and growth trajectory.
cards.use_when: Evaluating an agency or service business for sale, or planning an exit strategy for a services firm.

cards.title: Compounding returns of long-term specialization
cards.summary: A strategy for maximizing wealth: do what you're good at for an extremely long period to become world-class, rather than chasing fast money.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate time and energy across ventures, especially when tempted by quick-return opportunities like crypto or speculative investing.

cards.title: Build in public: how a speech impediment became a YouTube presence
cards.summary: A creator's method for overcoming public-speaking anxiety by starting on camera, then translating that to live leadership.
cards.use_when: Founders or operators who struggle with public speaking, video content, or addressing teams and need a desensitization approach.

cards.title: Do what you're good at, not what you're passionate about (early on)
cards.summary: A reframe of the 'follow your passion' advice: build competency and profit first, then pursue passion once financially free.
cards.use_when: Giving or receiving career advice for young people or early-stage founders, especially when choosing between a passion project and a practical income path.

cards.title: Billionaire habits: the one common denominator
cards.summary: Observing that sustained, long-term ambition to create money is the only consistent trait among billionaires; other factors vary widely.
cards.use_when: Analyzing high-net-worth individuals or deciding whether extreme wealth accumulation is the right goal for you.

cards.title: Fake it till you make it: situational and growth-oriented
cards.summary: A nuanced take on imposter syndrome and exaggeration: useful when non-malicious and directed toward building real capability.
cards.use_when: When feeling insecure in a new role or venture, or when assessing whether to project confidence you don't yet feel.

cards.title: Two foundations for reduced anxiety: truthfulness and confronting approval-seeking
cards.summary: The source's personal practices for greater peace: living 100% truthfully and examining why you care about others' opinions.
cards.use_when: Founders or high-performers experiencing anxiety, insecurity, or people-pleasing that affects decision-making.

cards.title: Spot product gaps by pairing search volume with a weak average rating
cards.summary: Use trend data to find sub-niches with high demand but poor existing product execution, flagged by a low average Amazon rating.
cards.use_when: Screening a product category or sub-niche for a viable entry point before committing to sourcing.

cards.title: Run an agent prompt that extracts and ranks unmet pain points
cards.summary: Prompt the AI agent to pull customer complaints from reviews, forums and Amazon Q&A, cluster them by theme and rank by urgency and willingness to pay.
cards.use_when: You have picked a category and need a defensible list of what customers actually want fixed before designing a product.

cards.title: Translate consumer language into manufacturing terminology before contacting suppliers
cards.summary: Use the AI agent to convert consumer-desired outcomes into precise manufacturing terms so supplier quotes reflect real specifications.
cards.use_when: Drafting a request for quote or first supplier message for a product whose quality depends on process details.

cards.title: Filter suppliers with a structured sourcing prompt
cards.summary: Specify OEM service, private label, MOQ ceiling and certifications in one prompt to get a shortlist instead of an overwhelming marketplace search.
cards.use_when: You have a validated product concept and need candidate manufacturers rather than browsing Alibaba manually.

cards.title: Score opportunities on wholesale-to-retail margin before designing
cards.summary: The sourcing tool reports wholesale cost, target retail price and gross margin percentage so you can compare product ideas on economics, not just demand.
cards.use_when: Choosing between several validated product ideas, or sanity-checking that a category can support the ad and fulfilment costs of ecommerce.

cards.title: Generate visual product concepts for a specific sub-demographic
cards.summary: Prompt the AI for brand identity, product line and visual mockups aimed at a narrow audience to test positioning before any manufacturing spend.
cards.use_when: You have a validated niche and a rough audience but no concrete product concept or brand direction.

cards.title: Vet shortlisted suppliers with three technical questions before ordering
cards.summary: Ask a small number of verification questions that expose whether a supplier can actually meet the differentiating specification.
cards.use_when: You have an AI-generated supplier shortlist and are about to contact them for the first time.

cards.title: Use agentic research to move from trend to concept, but keep human verification in the loop
cards.summary: AI agents compress market analysis, pain-point extraction and concept generation into one workflow, while sourcing decisions still require human checks.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much of an ecommerce product research workflow to delegate to an AI agent and where to intervene.

cards.title: Private supplier vs. AliExpress: understand the middleman model
cards.summary: A private supplier is a middleman who sources from Chinese factories/1688, routes goods through their own warehouse, then ships to your customer with better speed and pricing than public marketplaces.
cards.use_when: Deciding which fulfillment route to use for a dropshipping store, or explaining supply-chain options before sourcing a product

cards.title: Request the right shipping line to balance cost and speed
cards.summary: Choose a premium shipping line that keeps delivery inside roughly 6-10 days without overpaying, because slow delivery drives chargebacks.
cards.use_when: Configuring fulfillment with a private supplier or 3PL, or evaluating whether a quoted shipping cost is acceptable

cards.title: Get the product quote low enough that retail pricing stays viable
cards.summary: COGS is a primary lever on net margin — negotiate supplier quotes down and track how small per-unit savings compound across order volume.
cards.use_when: Quoting a product with a supplier, setting retail price, or reviewing net margin after a test

cards.title: Add branded packaging once a product is proven
cards.summary: Custom logos, mailers and thank-you inserts turn a commodity dropship item into a defensible brand and reduce undercutting.
cards.use_when: A product has validated sales and you want to protect margin from copycat competitors

cards.title: Add your fulfillment app as a Shopify location or checkout breaks
cards.summary: After installing a 3PL app you must manually register it as a Shopify fulfillment location, otherwise the storefront shows out-of-stock or add-to-cart failures.
cards.use_when: Setting up a new fulfillment/3PL integration on Shopify

cards.title: Pre-fund a 3PL wallet so orders fulfill automatically
cards.summary: Fulfillment networks debit a pre-funded balance as Shopify orders arrive, removing manual order entry; top up by bank transfer/wire.
cards.use_when: Automating order fulfillment after connecting a private supplier or 3PL to Shopify

cards.title: Source products through an agent on WhatsApp
cards.summary: A dedicated agent can source a product from a photo or marketplace link and return a quote, giving beginners support that public marketplaces lack.
cards.use_when: You have identified a product to sell but need a supplier quote, or you need help resolving a fulfillment issue

cards.title: Why the source rejects subscription fulfillment platforms and raw marketplaces
cards.summary: The presenter argues AliExpress/Alibaba and paid tools like AutoDS/Zendrop are poor options vs. a free private-supplier platform, on grounds of speed, branding, support and monthly fees.
cards.use_when: Choosing between marketplace dropshipping, paid fulfillment SaaS, and a private supplier/agent

cards.title: Judge net margin and refunds as the real supply-chain KPI
cards.summary: Low COGS plus reliable, traceable delivery protects net margin and prevents revenue loss to refunds and chargebacks.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether a supplier or shipping line is worth keeping

cards.title: Competitor profit as the primary product-viability filter
cards.summary: Treat active, profitable competitors as proof of concept rather than a disqualifying sign of saturation.
cards.use_when: Choosing whether to pursue a product or brushing off one because 'everyone is selling it'.

cards.title: Separating evergreen and trending products and the results each should deliver
cards.summary: Classify candidate products as evergreen (brand, slower start) or trending (fast cash, weeks-long window) because expectations and effort differ.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much testing budget and patience a product deserves before launching.

cards.title: Training a TikTok feed to surface dropshipping products
cards.summary: Use a fresh TikTok account, engage with blatant product-selling videos, and mine the feed for product candidates.
cards.use_when: You want low-cost product discovery from organic social rather than paid databases.

cards.title: One-hit-wonder check on a creator's profile
cards.summary: Before trusting a viral product video, audit the creator's profile for multiple high-view videos.
cards.use_when: A single viral video makes a product look promising and you need to know if it is repeatable or luck.

cards.title: PP Ads filter workflow: longest-running ads first
cards.summary: Reverse-engineer winning products from ad-spy tools by sorting for the longest-running creatives and excluding mega-brands.
cards.use_when: You want a repeatable pipeline of candidate products from paid ad intelligence.

cards.title: Estimating competitor revenue with a spy tool
cards.summary: Use a revenue estimator such as ShopHunter to confirm a product's sales before committing.
cards.use_when: You have a candidate product and want evidence that views or ads translate into actual sales.

cards.title: Facebook Ad Library keyword hunting for dropshippers
cards.summary: Find ecommerce advertisers and their products by searching generic direct-response keywords in the Facebook Ad Library.
cards.use_when: You want an unlimited free source of live competitor ads and product ideas.

cards.title: Reverse-sourcing a competitor product image to AliExpress
cards.summary: Use Google reverse image search on a competitor's product photo to find the raw supplier and margin floor.
cards.use_when: You have a validated product candidate and need to check sourcing cost and margin before committing.

cards.title: Anime katana worked example: validating a passionate-community product
cards.summary: A full walk-through of validating a non-problem-solving product because it serves a passionate niche community.
cards.use_when: A product does not solve a problem but clearly has an intense fan base; you need a validation sequence to follow.

cards.title: Customization products as a TikTok-friendly product class
cards.summary: Prefer customizable products because personalized items perform well in short-form product advertising.
cards.use_when: Scanning candidate lists and deciding which product types to shortlist for organic or paid testing.

cards.title: Deploying a saturated seasonal product with proven demand
cards.summary: When a product is heavily sold but repeatedly proves out, a short seasonal test can still be worthwhile even if it will not become a brand.
cards.use_when: You see the same product sold by many accounts and want a fast, low-ambition test rather than a long-term brand.

cards.title: Auxiliary product-discovery sources worth sampling
cards.summary: Supplementary channels — Twitter/X practitioners and trend sites — for finding product ideas, with quality caveats.
cards.use_when: Your main TikTok and ad-spy pipelines feel exhausted and you want additional idea inputs.

cards.title: The validation checklist applied to every product before selling
cards.summary: A repeatable gate: proof of competitors making money, demand signals, sourcing price and fulfillment readiness.
cards.use_when: Right before committing money or building a store around a product.

cards.title: Kalodata baseline filter settings for early-breakout products
cards.summary: Configuring the Kalodata/Shop Plus product screen (timeframe, revenue band, video-only attribution, ascending sort) to surface untapped TikTok Shop winners instead of saturated giants.
cards.use_when: Starting a product hunt in Kalodata or Shop Plus (accessed via Spy Crew) and needing a repeatable first-pass filter before graph analysis.

cards.title: Validate a product's growth curve with 30-day and 180-day graphs
cards.summary: Reading the 30-day upward tilt, then immediately checking the 180-day view to reject products that peaked months ago and are now dying.
cards.use_when: After a Kalodata/Shop Plus candidate passes the revenue-band filter, to decide whether it is genuinely climbing or a dead product attempting a revival.

cards.title: Check revenue distribution across recent videos, not one old viral hit
cards.summary: Inspecting a product's top videos to confirm revenue comes from multiple recent creatives rather than a single aged anomaly that will not repeat.
cards.use_when: When a Kalodata/Shop Plus product looks promising on the graph and you need to verify the revenue is repeatable with new creative.

cards.title: Cross-reference TikTok demand with Google Trends and Meta Ad Library
cards.summary: Validating a TikTok Shop candidate off-platform by searching the exact sub-niche in Google Trends and counting competitors running Meta ads.
cards.use_when: Before committing to sourcing or a paid test, to confirm demand is not confined to TikTok's algorithmic bubble.

cards.title: The sourcing criteria stack: problem-solving, English ads, renewable demand
cards.summary: The qualitative screen applied alongside Kalodata's numeric filters — problem/insecurity angle, English-language creative, repeat-purchase potential, and margin-friendly pricing.
cards.use_when: Choosing between several candidates that already pass the revenue, graph and video-distribution filters.

cards.title: Mix-and-match sourcing: borrow a viral TikTok hook, attach your own UGC body
cards.summary: A testing setup that takes a proven native TikTok hook from a top video and stitches it to a longer convincing UGC body for Meta ads.
cards.use_when: Once a product has passed sourcing validation and you are preparing the first Meta test creative.

cards.title: Keep sourcing, creative, media buying and storefront as separate decisions
cards.summary: Drawing scope boundaries so the product-research phase stays about trend and demand validation rather than drifting into ad editing, campaign setup or store design.
cards.use_when: Running or delegating a TikTok Shop product hunt and needing to know where the sourcing job ends.

cards.title: TikTok Shop product screening criteria (Baseline)
cards.summary: A seven-point filter for screening TikTok Shop products for dropshipping tests, including renewable potential, problem-solving angle, ad age, revenue trend and range, and English-speaking market.
cards.use_when: Screening a raw list of TikTok Shop products in a research tool (Kalodata/Shop Plus) before committing budget to a test.

cards.title: Reading 30-day vs 180-day revenue graphs in Kalodata
cards.summary: How to use the 30-day graph to spot uptrends, then immediately switch to 180-day data to reject products that peaked months ago.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a product's visible growth in the default research-tool view is real momentum or a dying product that only looks alive in a short window.

cards.title: Video age and revenue distribution checks
cards.summary: Validate a product by requiring a top-performing video posted in the last 7–14 days and revenue spread across at least three to five recent videos rather than one old hero video.
cards.use_when: After a product passes the revenue-graph screen, before deciding whether you have enough proven creative to build an ad test.

cards.title: Filtering out live-sales and cheap-impulse products
cards.summary: Reject TikTok Shop products whose revenue comes primarily from live streams or whose price point depends on cheap impulse buying.
cards.use_when: Screening candidate products in Kalodata and interpreting price and revenue-source data.

cards.title: Using revenue filters and the law of diminishing returns
cards.summary: How to set and adjust the revenue range filter based on whether previous tests produced profitable or unprofitable sales.
cards.use_when: Setting the revenue range in Kalodata and iterating on it after a test result.

cards.title: Validating a sub-niche trend on Google Trends
cards.summary: Validate that the exact product variation — not the broad category — has an active 12-month upward trajectory on Google Trends.
cards.use_when: After a specific product passes tool screening and you want trend confirmation before testing, especially for emerging formats like patches.

cards.title: Competition assessment via Facebook Ad Library and Page Transparency
cards.summary: Assess how many direct competitors are running the product, how long they've been running, and whether their stores and offers look beatable.
cards.use_when: Validating saturation and competitive positioning right before you decide to buy or build the store.

cards.title: Spy Crew as a budget alternative to full-price research tools
cards.summary: Use Spy Crew's bundled browser and tool access to get Kalodata, Shop Plus, PP Spy and other research utilities at a lower monthly cost than subscribing separately.
cards.use_when: Setting up a research stack when Kalodata's standalone price is the constraint.

cards.title: Searching for the most untapped products: sort and ignore images
cards.summary: In the product list, sort revenue lowest to highest and screen on graph shape first, using product images only to spot known-saturated items.
cards.use_when: Starting a live hunt in Kalodata and deciding which rows to click into.

cards.title: Reading stacked hooks that introduce a novel ingredient or format
cards.summary: How branded ingredient or unusual format claims (liposomal, NAD, patches) create perceived sophistication and a reason to click.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether a supplement or wellness product has a defensible angle beyond a commodity ingredient.

cards.title: Translating a TikTok-native creative into a Meta ad (mix-match)
cards.summary: Combine a validated short TikTok hook with a longer, more convincing creator body to produce a Meta-optimized ad.
cards.use_when: Building your first ad set after buying a validated product, especially when the top TikTok video is a very short viral clip.

cards.title: Acting on brand-new videos to get ahead of a spike
cards.summary: Use very recent video posting dates and rapid view velocity as an early-entry signal before a product saturates, and accept the gamble that comes with it.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to move immediately on a product whose graph is rising steeply and whose top videos were posted days ago.

cards.title: Pricing and offer strategy when translating a cheap TikTok product to Meta
cards.summary: Raise price and build an offer structure on your own store because Meta audiences respond to longer, more convincing ad-to-site experiences.
cards.use_when: You have validated a low-priced TikTok Shop product (e.g. $15) and need a viable offer for a Meta funnel.

cards.title: Choosing a niche based on business model
cards.summary: Pick your research category according to whether you want recurring revenue or high-volume one-off sales.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to hunt in Kalodata's category filter before starting a product search.

cards.title: Read short-term spikes as gambling products
cards.summary: Distinguish 'gamble' products that blow up just recently from products with sustained revenue history.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a product whose revenue graph shows a recent sharp spike, before committing to test it.

cards.title: Lower revenue filters to cut competitive products
cards.summary: Narrowing the revenue band to roughly $36K-$70K surfaces less saturated products than a $70K+ band.
cards.use_when: The product list is full of products you've seen advertised many times, or you want less competitive candidates.

cards.title: Screen out non-English creatives before testing
cards.summary: Products whose winning content is in Spanish are a hard skip because they don't transfer to English-speaking audiences.
cards.use_when: Checking a product's top-performing videos during research.

cards.title: Check how concentrated the winning videos are
cards.summary: Revenue spread across several videos is healthier than one dominant winning video.
cards.use_when: Judging whether a candidate product's recent sales are repeatable across creative.

cards.title: Competitor-set your niche, not just your product
cards.summary: When you sell a variant format you still compete with every other format of the same ingredient or niche.
cards.use_when: Assessing saturation for supplement-style or format-substitution products.

cards.title: Pressure-test the offer before you sell the same product
cards.summary: Competitor offers often bundle a commodity product into a branded kit; copyable offer structure matters as much as the product.
cards.use_when: You found a product with an appealing graph but generic positioning, and need a differentiation angle.

cards.title: Skip products with low perceived-value pricing
cards.summary: Under-$10 price points force matching price and usually fail the perceived-value test.
cards.use_when: A researched product shows a good graph but sells cheaply.

cards.title: Use the shape of the 180-day graph as a fast filter
cards.summary: Up-down-up with an overall uptrend is healthy; a graph already in the gutter or on a downtrend is not worth testing.
cards.use_when: Scanning many products and deciding which ones deserve a closer look.

cards.title: Research candidates against Facebook Ad Library and Google Trends
cards.summary: A product counts as validated when it survives both a competitor search and a trend check.
cards.use_when: You have a candidate with a good graph and need a go/no-go before testing.

cards.title: Switch filter categories to find cross-listed winners
cards.summary: A product can appear under a different dashboard category than the niche it truly belongs to, so loosen category filters.
cards.use_when: You are searching a niche and the category filter may be hiding relevant products.

cards.title: Choose niches by competition level, not popularity
cards.summary: Beauty and personal care equals health in potential but also in competition; less-hyped niches like home, tools and appliances often have lower competition.
cards.use_when: Deciding which niche to hunt in before opening the product dashboard.

cards.title: Beware recognizable products and brands
cards.summary: If you've seen the product or brand many times — in ads or as an established retailer — pass on it.
cards.use_when: A candidate looks familiar or comes from a long-established brand.

cards.title: Decide whether to keep hunting or switch niches
cards.summary: If pages of results are duds, adjust filters or switch niche rather than quitting early.
cards.use_when: You have scrolled several result pages without a candidate worth testing.

cards.title: Accept that validated products can still fail your test
cards.summary: Testing a validated product on Meta with your own ads and offer is a new experiment, not a guaranteed win.
cards.use_when: Planning a product test after research signals look strong.

cards.title: Run a 16-question validation pass before sourcing any physical product
cards.summary: A structured 16-point checklist that screens a product idea across market, competition, economics, logistics and retention before you spend on inventory.
cards.use_when: You have a physical product idea and want an objective go/no-go screen before committing time, sourcing spend or manufacturing.

cards.title: Size demand with Keyword Planner search volume plus social mention volume
cards.summary: Use free search-volume and social-listening tools to estimate whether enough people are actively looking for the product before investing.
cards.use_when: You need a first quantitative read on demand for a product concept and have not yet chosen suppliers.

cards.title: Classify the market direction: growing, flat, fad or declining
cards.summary: Use Google Trends and trend research to separate a durable upward category from a passing fad or a market you have already missed.
cards.use_when: Demand volume looks acceptable and you need to judge whether the category will still exist in two to three years.

cards.title: Map competitors, including free and DIY substitutes
cards.summary: Research the competitive landscape in your target markets, treating grocery-store alternatives and homemade substitutes as real competitors.
cards.use_when: You are validating a product category and want to know whether there is room for a new entrant.

cards.title: Profile target customers before committing to a product
cards.summary: Estimate who the buyers are, where they live and whether they buy online, so you do not discover unshippable or unreachable demand too late.
cards.use_when: You need to confirm the product's audience is reachable and in a country you can ship to and advertise in.

cards.title: Target the $50–$150 retail price band for paid-acquisition economics
cards.summary: A commonly cited sweet spot where a product carries enough margin to fund paid ads but is not so expensive that buyers expect premium service.
cards.use_when: You are choosing between product concepts or setting an initial retail price for a product you intend to acquire customers for with paid ads.
